history.heading: Korean kingdoms
paragraphs: The Korean Peninsula has a long shared history. According to legend, Gojoseon was founded in 2333 BCE. The Three Kingdoms period saw Goguryeo, which ruled much of the north and Manchuria, Baekje and Silla. Later dynasties, Goryeo (918–1392) and Joseon (1392–1910), unified the peninsula. Pyongyang was the capital of Goguryeo.
Japan annexed Korea in 1910 and ruled it harshly until 1945.

history.heading: Division and the Korean War
paragraphs: At the end of the Second World War, the Soviet Union occupied the north and the United States the south. In 1948 two states were proclaimed: the Democratic People's Republic of Korea in the north, led by Kim Il Sung, and the Republic of Korea in the south.

In 1950 North Korea invaded the South, starting the Korean War. US-led UN forces and Chinese troops intervened, and the war killed millions before an armistice in 1953, which left the peninsula divided along the heavily fortified Demilitarized Zone. No peace treaty has been signed.

history.heading: The Kim dynasty
paragraphs: Kim Il Sung built a totalitarian state based on a personality cult and the ideology of Juche (self-reliance). His son Kim Jong Il succeeded him in 1994; a famine in the 1990s killed hundreds of thousands. Kim Jong Un has ruled since 2011.

North Korea has developed nuclear weapons, conducting six nuclear tests since 2006, and long-range missiles, leading to UN sanctions. Summits with US President Donald Trump in 2018–19 produced no lasting agreement. In 2024 North Korea declared South Korea its "principal enemy" and abandoned the goal of reunification, and it sent troops to fight for Russia against Ukraine.

culture.heading: State-controlled culture
paragraphs: Korean is the official language. Culture is tightly controlled by the state and centred on glorifying the Kim family, with monuments, mass games and propaganda art. Religion is severely restricted.

Traditional Korean culture, such as kimchi-making (recognised by UNESCO in its North Korean form) and Pyongyang cold noodles (naengmyeon), remains important. Access to foreign media is a serious crime.

politics.heading: Totalitarian state
paragraphs: North Korea is one of the most closed and repressive states in the world. Power is held by Kim Jong Un, leader of the Workers' Party of Korea and the state. Elections offer only a single approved candidate. A UN inquiry found crimes against humanity, including a system of political prison camps. Travel abroad and access to information are tightly restricted.
North Korea's main allies are China and Russia, with which it signed a mutual defence treaty in 2024.

economy.heading: Planned economy
paragraphs: North Korea has a centrally planned economy, though informal markets (jangmadang) have grown since the 1990s famine. It is one of the poorest countries in Asia, with chronic food shortages. Sanctions restrict exports of coal, minerals and textiles. China is its main trading partner, and the regime earns money through arms sales, cybertheft of cryptocurrency and overseas workers. The currency is the North Korean won.
